title: Hooks: the guard that never forgets

beats.say: What if your building had a security guard who never forgets, never sleeps, and never skips a check?

A hook is like that guard. Claude is the worker. Before the worker picks up a power tool, the guard checks the job. After the work is done, a cleaner tidies up. When the worker finishes the day, an inspector tests everything.
Each of these moments is called an event. Pre tool use is the guard at the door. Post tool use is the cleaner. Stop is the inspector.
The key point: asking Claude nicely is only a request. A hook is a rule. It runs every single time.

check.q: What is the main difference between telling Claude a rule in a prompt and using a hook?
opts: A hook runs every time its event happens
A hook makes Claude smarter
A prompt rule is always enforced
Hooks only run when Claude agrees
check.why: A prompt is a request Claude may miss. A hook is a script triggered by an event, so it runs every time.

work: List three rules you keep repeating to Claude and mark which could be a hook.
Decide for each rule whether it belongs before, after, or at the end of the work.

title: Hook events and how they are wired

beats.say: Which moment should a rule fire at: before an edit, or after it? That choice decides everything.
Pre tool use runs before a tool such as Bash, Edit or Write. It can deny the call, so risky commands never run. Post tool use runs after success, so it suits formatting, linting or logging.

User prompt submit fires when you send a prompt, and can add context or block secrets. Stop fires when Claude finishes. Session start loads the branch. Pre compact saves notes. Notification sends a desktop alert.

show.title: The other events
items: Stop: run tests, ask Claude to continue

beats.say: You configure them in a settings file, user, project or local. A matcher like Bash pipe Edit pipe Write picks which tools trigger the command.

check.q: You want to stop Claude running a dangerous shell command. Which event do you use?
opts: PostToolUse
PreToolUse
Notification
SessionStart
check.why: Only PreToolUse runs before the tool and can deny it. PostToolUse fires after the command already ran.

work: Write a small PreToolUse hook that denies one risky Bash pattern.
Add a PostToolUse hook with an Edit or Write matcher to run your formatter.

title: Hook gotchas interviewers probe

beats.say: Your post tool use hook runs the tests, but a failing test never complains. Why?
The command pipes output into tail. A pipeline reports the exit code of its last command, and tail always succeeds. So the failure is hidden from the hook's status.

show.title: The masked failure
show.text:
python3 -m unittest -q 2>&1 | tail -5
# exit code comes from tail, not from unittest

beats.say: Timing matters too. Post tool use fires after the tool succeeded, so it cannot undo the edit. Only pre tool use can deny. If you need prevention, guard before, not after.
A stop hook that tells Claude to continue when tests fail can loop forever if the tests never pass. Add a limit or check a flag. Also, running a whole suite after every edit is slow.

show.title: More traps
items: Add a retry limit or flag
Full suite per edit is slow

check.q: A PostToolUse hook runs a test command piped into tail. Tests fail but the hook looks successful. What is the likely cause?
opts: PostToolUse ignores all failures
The pipeline exit code comes from tail
Matchers hide errors
Tests cannot run in hooks
check.why: A pipeline returns the status of its last command. tail succeeds, so the test failure is masked unless you preserve the exit code.

work: Check every hook command that pipes output and confirm the real exit code survives.
Add a retry cap to any Stop hook that asks Claude to keep going.

title: Designing a hook strategy

beats.say: Hooks are cheap guardrails, so why not put every rule in one?

show.text: Why not all rules in hooks?

beats.say: Every hook is a process spawned on each matching call. Heavy ones add latency to every edit and cost developer patience. Put fast checks on pre tool use, and slow ones like the full test suite on stop, once per turn.
Scope matters. Team rules go in project settings, committed to git. Personal preferences go in user or local settings.

show.title: Choose the scope
items: Project: shared team rules in git

beats.say: Hooks guard one agent session only. They don't replace branch protection, CI, or permissions, which hold even when a hook is missing. Use hooks for fast feedback, and CI as the final gate.

check.q: Where should a slow full test suite run to limit friction?
opts: PreToolUse on every call
PostToolUse on every edit
Stop, once per turn
SessionStart
check.why: Stop fires once when Claude finishes its turn, so slow checks run once instead of after every edit.

work: Time each hook and move anything slow from edit-level events to Stop.
Keep shared hooks in project settings and back them with CI checks.

title: A sign versus a lock

beats.say: A sign says please do not enter. A lock actually stops you. Which one would you trust to protect a safe?
A rule in the CLAUDE dot M D file is a sign. Claude reads it and usually obeys. But usually means that now and then, it does not.
A hook is the lock. It is a small program that Claude Code runs at a fixed moment, like just before a file is edited. It runs every time. The model gets no vote.
So keep notes for style and taste. Use hooks for secrets, production, and anything that cannot be undone.

check.q: Why is a rule in CLAUDE.md not enough to protect a secrets file?
opts: Claude cannot read the file
The model follows it usually, but nothing forces it every time
Markdown files are ignored on startup
check.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model weighs. A hook is code that runs at a fixed point regardless of what the model decides.

work: List the three things Claude must never touch in your repo, such as secrets, production and destructive commands.
Move any rule from that list out of CLAUDE.md prose and into a hook.
Keep style preferences in CLAUDE.md, where flexibility is fine.

title: What happens when a hook fires

beats.say: What actually happens when Claude tries to edit your dot env file?

Claude Code reaches a fixed point in its loop, for example just before a tool runs. It looks up your hooks in settings and starts your command, passing details about the call as JSON on standard input.

Your script reads the file path. If it ends in dot env, it prints a reason and exits with code two. Exit code two means block. The edit never happens, and Claude sees your reason and picks another route.
Exit zero lets the call go ahead. The check is plain code, so it costs milliseconds and gives the same answer every time.

check.q: A before-tool hook exits with code two. What happens?
opts: The tool call runs and the error is logged
The tool call is blocked and Claude sees the reason
Claude Code shuts down
check.why: Exit code two is the blocking signal. The tool does not run, and the message you printed is fed back so Claude can adjust.

work: Write a small script that reads the tool input JSON and blocks any path ending in .env.
Test it by hand with sample JSON and check that it exits 2 on a match and 0 otherwise.
Print a clear reason so Claude knows what to do instead.

title: Why the secret still leaked

beats.say: Your hook blocks edits to dot env. So how can a secret still leak?

Because a hook only guards the event it watches. If you match only the edit tool, Claude can still run a shell command like cat or sed on the same file. Match every tool that can reach it, and check the command text too.

Other gotchas. A hook that crashes with some other error code does not block; only exit code two does. A slow hook delays every call, so keep it fast. And a hook runs with your permissions, so treat its script like production code.

show.title: Hook gotchas
items: Only exit 2 blocks; other errors just warn
Match every tool that can reach the target

check.q: Your hook blocks the edit tool on .env, yet the file contents leak. Most likely cause?
opts: Exit code zero means block
The shell tool can read the file and is not hooked
Hooks only run once per session
check.why: A hook guards only what it matches. The shell tool offers another route, so cover it and inspect command text.

work: Audit which tools can read or write each protected path, not just the edit tool.
Make failures explicit: test that your script exits 2 on bad input, not some other code.
Time your hooks and keep each to milliseconds.

title: Where hooks stop being the answer

beats.say: If hooks are so strong, why not put every rule in one?

Because each hook adds latency to every call and one more script to maintain. Reserve hooks for rules where a miss is costly: secrets, production deploys, destructive commands. Leave style and preferences to CLAUDE dot M D, which is free and flexible.

show.title: Spend hooks where a miss is *costly*

chip.text: Enforce only what must not fail

beats.say: Also, a hook is a guardrail, not a security boundary. A determined path around it may exist. Back it with real controls: least privilege credentials, read only database roles, and protected branches. Put shared hooks in checked in project settings so the whole team gets the same rules.

check.q: Which is the best use of a hook rather than a CLAUDE.md note?
opts: Preferring tabs over spaces
Blocking any command that drops a production table
Suggesting a naming style for tests
check.why: Hooks suit rules where one miss is costly. Style is cheap to get wrong and fits guidance. Pair hooks with real permissions too.

work: Rank your rules by cost of a miss and hook only the top tier.
Back each hook with real controls such as read only roles and protected branches.
Commit shared hooks to project settings and review them like production code.

title: The guard at the door

beats.say: How do you stop a helpful assistant from doing something dangerous, even when it forgets the rules?
Picture a security guard at a door. Before anyone walks through, the guard reads a note: who they are, and what they want to do.
If the request is fine, the guard nods and waves them through. If it is risky, the guard says stop, and explains why in a short note.
The assistant reads that note and tries a safer way. A hook is that guard. It always runs, so it never forgets.

check.q: Why is a hook like a guard at a door, rather than a reminder note?
opts: It checks every action before it happens, whether or not the assistant remembers
It makes the assistant smarter
It only runs when the assistant asks for it
check.why: A guard checks every request automatically. A reminder can be forgotten, but a hook always runs.

work: List three actions in your project that you would want a guard to stop.
Write down, in plain words, what reason message would help the assistant pick a safer way.

title: Input in, exit code out

beats.say: How does a tiny script decide whether an AI tool call may run?

Before the tool runs, the hook receives a JSON message on standard input. It holds the event name, the tool name, and the tool input. For a Bash call, that input is the command. For an edit, it is the file path.
The script answers with its exit code. Zero means carry on. Two means block. Any other code is a non-blocking error, shown to you, and the call still goes ahead.

show.title: Exit codes
items: Anything else: error shown to you, call still runs

beats.say: When you block, whatever you print on standard error goes back to Claude. So write a clear reason, and it can adjust and try again.

check.q: A PreToolUse hook should cancel the tool call and tell Claude why. What should it do?
opts: Print the reason on stdout and exit 0
Print the reason on stderr and exit 2
Print the reason on stderr and exit 1
check.why: Exit 2 blocks the call, and stderr is what Claude sees. Exit 1 is a non-blocking error, so the call would still run.

work: Log the raw JSON a hook receives for a Bash call and an Edit call, and read the fields.
Write one guard that exits 2 with a one-sentence reason.

title: When a guard fails open

beats.say: Your guard script crashes and exits with code one. Did it block the dangerous command?

No. Only exit code two blocks. A crash, a typo, or a missing module gives another code, which is a non-blocking error. The dangerous call still runs. So catch errors, and decide on purpose whether to exit two.

Next, patterns are fragile. A search for dot env catches the obvious file, but a command can build the name from pieces. Match drop in any letter case, and with word boundaries, so it does not flag a column called dropdown.

show.title: Regex gotchas
items: Use word boundaries to avoid false alarms

beats.say: Finally, print the reason on standard error, not standard output. On a block, only standard error reaches Claude.

check.q: Your hook has a bug and raises an uncaught exception, exiting with code one. What happens to a dangerous Bash command?
opts: It is blocked, because the hook failed
It still runs, because exit 1 is non-blocking
Claude is asked to confirm it
check.why: Only exit code 2 blocks. Other codes are non-blocking errors, so a buggy guard fails open unless you handle errors and exit 2.

work: Wrap your guard in a try block and decide whether errors should exit 2.
Test your patterns with upper case, extra spaces and odd quoting.
Check that your block message goes to stderr.

title: Hooks are a tripwire, not a vault

beats.say: Is a hook script enough to protect production?

No. A hook is a tripwire that always runs, which beats a prompt rule the model can forget. But pattern matching is a blocklist, and blocklists leak. Real protection is least privilege: a database login that cannot drop tables, and no secrets on disk.
Hooks run on every tool call, so keep them fast, well under a second, and avoid network calls.
Start with exit codes. Move to JSON decisions, allow, deny or ask, when a human should confirm rather than face a hard block. Keep the hook in the repository so every teammate gets the same guard.

show.title: Rollout
items: JSON allow, deny or ask for nuance

check.q: What is the strongest way to stop an agent dropping a production table?
opts: A hook regex for the word DROP
A prompt that says never drop tables
A database login without drop rights, plus the hook as a backup
check.why: Least privilege cannot be bypassed by rewording a command. The hook is a useful extra layer, but a blocklist alone leaks.

work: Audit which credentials your agent can reach, and remove write rights it does not need.
Keep hooks under a fraction of a second and free of network calls.
Commit shared hooks to the repo and review them like code.

title: A hook is a script wearing your keys

beats.say: Imagine a stranger hands you a checklist and says, follow this every morning, using your own house keys. Would you read it first?

show.sub: A checklist that uses your keys

beats.say: A hook is exactly that. It is a small script that runs automatically whenever Claude is about to do something. It runs as you, with your keys, your files, and your passwords. So it can do anything you can do.

That is why you read a hook like production code, and never install one from a repo you do not trust. A good hook is like a smoke alarm. Fast, silent when all is fine, and loud only when something is wrong.

show.title: A good hook is a smoke alarm
items: Never install from a repo you do not trust
Loud only when something is wrong

check.q: Why should you review a hook script before installing it?
opts: It runs with your own permissions, so it can do what you can do
It only runs once a year
It runs in a locked box with no access to files
It is always written by Claude, so it is safe
check.why: Hooks run as you. A bad or malicious hook has your files, credentials and access, so review it like production code.

work: List the hooks active in your current project and read each script once.
Before cloning an unfamiliar repo, check whether it ships hook settings.
Write a one-line rule for your team: no hooks from untrusted repos.

title: Pipe-test the guard

beats.say: How do you know your safety hook really blocks anything, before it matters?

Claude passes the hook a small JSON message on standard input, naming the tool and the command. Your script reads it, decides, and exits with a number. Exit zero means allow. Exit two means block, and the message you print explains why.
So test it by hand. Echo a fake rm minus rf command into your script, then print the exit code. You should see the reason and the number two. If you see zero, your guard is decoration.
Do it before you trust it, not after the first accident.

check.q: You pipe a dangerous command into your guard and the exit code prints 0. What does that mean?
opts: The guard blocked it successfully
The guard allowed it, so the block logic is not working
The guard crashed and Claude stopped
The command was too short to check
check.why: Exit zero means allow. A working guard should print its reason and exit with 2 for a dangerous command.

work: Pipe-test every guard with one command it should block and one it should allow.
Keep the test command in a README next to the hook script.
Print a clear reason on block so Claude can adjust.

title: When a guard fails open

beats.say: Your guard script crashes. Does Claude stop, or carry on? Carry on, and that is the trap.

Only exit code two blocks. A crash, such as a typo or a missing Python module, usually exits with one. That counts as a plain error, not a block, so the dangerous command goes through. This is called failing open. Test the block path, not just the happy path.
Stop hooks have a loop risk. If a check fails and tells Claude to keep working, and it always fails, Claude never finishes. Add a limit, such as three tries.
Use the hooks command to see what is actually active.

check.q: Your guard script has a typo and exits with code 1 on every call. What happens to dangerous commands?
opts: They are blocked, because any non-zero code blocks
They are blocked only for Bash
They go through, because only exit code 2 blocks
Claude is shut down
check.why: Exit 1 is a non-blocking error, so the guard fails open. Only exit 2 blocks, which is why you must test the block path.

work: Wrap guard logic so unexpected errors are logged loudly and tested.
Add a retry counter to any Stop hook that tells Claude to continue.
Run the hooks command after each settings change to confirm what is live.

title: Hooks are guardrails, not walls

beats.say: If a hook adds two hundred milliseconds, what does that cost over a long session?
A session with five hundred matching calls loses a hundred seconds. So keep hooks fast: match narrowly, avoid network calls, and stay silent on success.
Also know the limit. A hook runs as you, so it is a guardrail, not a wall. A bug or a malicious script has all your permissions. For hard isolation, use a sandbox or a container with least privilege.

chip.text: Use a sandbox for hard limits

beats.say: Treat hooks as shared code: review them, version them, pin them, and never inherit them blindly from an unfamiliar repo.

check.q: What is the best control when you need strong isolation from a possibly untrusted agent?
opts: A longer hook script
A hook that prints more warnings
A sandbox or container with least privilege
Running the hook twice
check.why: Hooks run with your permissions, so they are guardrails. Real isolation needs an environment that limits what can be reached at all.

work: Measure hook runtime and keep each one well under a hundred milliseconds.
Put shared hooks in a reviewed repo with owners, not copied around by hand.
Run risky agent work in a sandbox and use hooks as an extra layer.
